title: Vincent de Paul and Louise de Marillac
hook: a priest and a widow organize charity for the poor of Paris

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis de Sales, the gentleman saint. Your line was nothing so strong as gentleness.

One Sunday in a French country parish, just before the sermon, the priest hears that a whole family nearby is sick, with no one to look after them. He tells the congregation. That afternoon, the story goes, people stream down the road with soup, bread and blankets. Too much, all at once. Some of the food goes to waste, and by next week the family could be alone again. Kindness had shown up, but nobody had organized it. So the priest writes a simple plan: who goes on which day, what they bring, how they speak to the sick. That priest was Vincent de Paul.

The plan grew. Groups of women in parish after parish took turns visiting the sick poor, and Vincent needed someone to hold it all together. He found her in Louise de Marillac, a widow with a sharp mind and, tradition says, a long struggle with anxiety and doubt of her own. She traveled to the groups, checked on them, trained them, and wrote to Vincent about what was working. Together they gathered young women into a community that came to be called the Daughters of Charity. They were not to live behind convent walls, but out among people: in hospitals, in homes, with orphans, in the streets of Paris. Vincent is remembered for putting it this way: their cloister would be the streets of the city. The reason sits in Matthew's Gospel, where Jesus says: "I was sick, and ye visited me". And then: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." Today's line is linked to Vincent too: the poor are our masters. It flips the usual picture. The helper isn't the one in charge. The people being served are the ones to be honored, listened to and waited on, the way a good servant attends to a household. Catholics honor both as saints, and the Daughters of Charity still serve today.
screen: `I WAS SICK, AND YE VISITED ME.`

segments.voice: Think of who near you needs help: a food bank, a shelter, a sick neighbor, someone at a care home who rarely gets visitors. Pick one, and do what Vincent did: make it concrete, which day, what time, what you'd bring. Then let the plan go and breathe; if you pray, rest with the words I was sick, and ye visited me, and if not, with the face of the person you'd serve.
Vincent. The priest who turned scattered kindness into organized care for the poor of Paris, working with Louise de Marillac to send women out to serve in the streets.
Your line: the poor are our masters. Kindness, given a plan. That's day eight hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Vincent de Paul and Louise de Marillac as saints; the Daughters of Charity and the lay Society of Saint Vincent de Paul carry on their work, and parish groups named for him run visits and food pantries.

chat.meaning: When too much help came at once and then faded, Vincent wrote a simple plan: who goes on which day, what they bring, how they speak.
